title: Epiglottitis (thumbprint sign): Haemophilus influenzae (gram-negative coccobacilli)
vignette: A 10-year-old boy is brought to the emergency department due to respiratory distress. Over the past 6 hours, rapid, noisy breathing has progressively developed. Temperature is 40.1 C (104.2 F), blood pressure is 105/75 mm Hg, pulse is 120/min, and respirations are 32/min. Examination shows inspiratory stridor and supraclavicular retractions. A lateral neck x-ray shows a swollen epiglottis ('thumbprint sign'). The patient is admitted to the hospital, and blood cultures are obtained. If blood cultures are positive, which of the following would most likely be seen on Gram stain?

clues.text: rapid, noisy breathing has progressively developed
clues.note: Rapidly progressive stridor with high fever and toxicity suggests epiglottitis - a potentially fatal upper-airway infection.
Inspiratory stridor and retractions signal upper-airway obstruction from a swollen epiglottis.
The 'thumbprint sign' (enlarged epiglottis) on lateral neck x-ray is characteristic of epiglottitis; the most common cause is Haemophilus influenzae.

whatMatters: Rapidly progressive stridor, high fever, and a 'THUMBPRINT SIGN' (swollen epiglottis) = EPIGLOTTITIS. The most common cause (and one that often causes concomitant bacteremia) is HAEMOPHILUS INFLUENZAE - a GRAM-NEGATIVE COCCOBACILLUS on Gram stain. Answer B.
strategy: Recognize epiglottitis and its top pathogen: Haemophilus influenzae (type b historically; now nontypeable/type b with waning immunity), a gram-negative coccobacillus, which frequently seeds the blood. Reject gram-negative cocci (Moraxella/Neisseria - rare here), gram-negative rods in chains (Klebsiella - rare), gram-positive cocci in chains (S. pneumoniae) and clusters (S. aureus) - less common causes of epiglottitis, and less likely to be the blood-culture organism than H. influenzae.

eliminations.label: Gram-negative cocci in pairs - Moraxella/Neisseria
eliminations.detail: WHAT IT IS: gram-negative diplococci (Moraxella, Neisseria). ❌ WHY IT FAILS: these are rare causes of epiglottitis and less likely on blood culture than H. influenzae. ✅ Correct if: Neisseria/Moraxella infection.

eliminations.label: Gram-negative rods in chains - Klebsiella
eliminations.detail: WHAT IT IS: gram-negative rods (e.g., Klebsiella). ❌ WHY IT FAILS: rare cause of epiglottitis; H. influenzae (coccobacillus) is the classic organism. ✅ Correct if: an enteric gram-negative rod infection.

eliminations.label: Gram-positive cocci in chains - Streptococcus pneumoniae
eliminations.detail: WHAT IT IS: streptococci (e.g., S. pneumoniae). ❌ WHY IT FAILS: although pneumococcal epiglottitis has increased since Hib vaccination, H. influenzae strains combined are still the most common, and Hib is more likely to cause the bacteremia. ✅ Correct if: pneumococcal epiglottitis with lancet-shaped diplococci.

eliminations.label: Gram-positive cocci in clusters - Staphylococcus aureus
eliminations.detail: WHAT IT IS: staphylococci (clusters). ❌ WHY IT FAILS: a less common cause of epiglottitis than H. influenzae. ✅ Correct if: staphylococcal infection.

reasoning: Rapidly progressive stridor + high fever + thumbprint sign = epiglottitis
The most common cause is Haemophilus influenzae, which often causes concomitant bacteremia
H. influenzae is a gram-negative coccobacillus on Gram stain
mechanism: Epiglottitis is inflammation/swelling of the epiglottis that can rapidly obstruct the upper airway (a medical emergency). Classic features are RAPIDLY progressive respiratory distress, high fever, drooling, dysphagia, a muffled 'hot potato' voice, the tripod position, and inspiratory stridor; the lateral neck x-ray shows an enlarged epiglottis - the 'THUMBPRINT SIGN.' Historically it occurred mainly in young children due to HAEMOPHILUS INFLUENZAE type b (Hib); with widespread Hib vaccination the incidence fell dramatically and now affects older children and adults more often, but H. INFLUENZAE (type b due to waning immunity plus nontypeable strains) remains the MOST COMMON cause. H. influenzae is a GRAM-NEGATIVE COCCOBACILLUS, and Hib epiglottitis is frequently associated with BACTEREMIA (its polysaccharide capsule is highly invasive), so blood cultures would show gram-negative coccobacilli. Management prioritizes securing the airway (do not agitate the child), plus antibiotics. The distractors (gram-negative cocci/rods, gram-positive cocci) represent less common causes and are less likely to be the blood-culture organism.

difficulty.label: 🧠 Knowledge
difficulty.text: First Aid Micro/ENT > epiglottitis: thumbprint sign, rapidly progressive stridor/drooling; #1 cause Haemophilus influenzae (gram-negative coccobacillus), often bacteremic; secure airway; Hib vaccine reduced incidence.

difficulty.label: 📖 Comprehension
difficulty.text: Epiglottitis (thumbprint sign) -> H. influenzae -> gram-negative coccobacilli on blood culture.

difficulty.label: 🔤 Vocab
difficulty.text: Unsure on epiglottitis, thumbprint sign, coccobacillus, or Haemophilus influenzae type b? Tell me which.

difficulty.label: 🨤 Distractor
difficulty.text: Gram-negative cocci (Moraxella/Neisseria), rods in chains (Klebsiella), and gram-positive cocci (strep/staph) are less common causes.

difficulty.label: 🖼️ Imaging / diagram
difficulty.text: On the lateral neck x-ray: an enlarged, rounded epiglottis (the 'thumbprint sign') obstructing the airway. Anchor: 'thumbprint = epiglottitis = H. influenzae (gram-negative coccobacilli).'

difficulty.label: 🗒️ Other
difficulty.text: Bank: epiglottitis = thumbprint sign; H. influenzae (gram-negative coccobacillus), often bacteremic; airway emergency.

keywords.back: Sharp decline in epiglottitis; now older children/adults

firstAid.detail: Micro: H. influenzae (gram-negative coccobacilli); thumbprint sign; bacteremia.
ENT > secure airway first; avoid agitating the child.

memoryHook: A high fever, drooling child with a 'thumbprint' epiglottis = epiglottitis - and the classic invader, H. influenzae, shows up as gram-negative coccobacilli in the blood.
